title: Repair hours
brief: Write the board decision memo for a neighborhood repair cooperative deciding its next six-month opening schedule. Last quarter: Tue noon 122 visits, Thu evening 178, Sat morning 243. Of 84 surveyed members, 35 wanted Sundays and 31 wanted weekday evenings; multiple answers allowed. The lease allows four opening days. Two volunteer captains can each cover one extra shift a fortnight; the paid coordinator already works 32 hours. A Sunday trial would cost 140 currency units per session. Budget for a trial: 1,200. Twelve partner referrals arrived when the shop was closed; time of arrival wasn't recorded. The board wants a decision it can take this month and a way to tell whether access actually improves.

65bec990d480e5fe.text:
# Board Decision Memo: Opening Schedule for the Next Six Months

**For decision at this month's board meeting**

## Decision requested

The board is asked to set the opening schedule for the next six months and to agree in advance how it will judge whether access has improved.

## Recommendation

Keep the three current sessions unchanged for the full six months, and add a weekly Sunday session as an eight-week trial.

- **Cost:** eight sessions at 140 each come to 1,120, inside the 1,200 trial budget, with 80 left over.
- **Staffing:** the two volunteer captains alternate Sundays, which uses exactly the extra shift per fortnight each has offered. The trial asks nothing more of the coordinator.
- **Lease:** Sunday becomes the fourth opening day, the maximum the lease allows.
- **Measurement:** from the first week of the new schedule, every session records whether each visitor could have come at another time, and every partner referral is logged with its day and time.
- **Review:** the board fixes the pass marks now and reviews the results at its first meeting after the eighth Sunday.

## What we know

Last quarter's attendance was as follows. The averages assume thirteen sessions of each type.

| Session | Visits last quarter | Average per session |
|---|---|---|
| Tuesday noon | 122 | about 9 |
| Thursday evening | 178 | about 14 |
| Saturday morning | 243 | about 19 |
| **Total** | **543** | **about 42 per week** |

**Member survey.** Of 84 members surveyed, 35 (42%) wanted Sundays and 31 (37%) wanted weekday evenings. Members could give more than one answer, so we do not know how many people are in both groups.

**Constraints.**

- The lease allows four opening days, and we use three.
- Each captain can cover one extra shift a fortnight, which together makes one extra session a week and no more.
- The coordinator already works 32 hours, and this memo treats those hours as fully committed.
- The trial budget is 1,200, and a Sunday session is costed at 140.

**Partner referrals.** Twelve referrals arrived last quarter when the shop was closed. Nobody recorded when they arrived, so we cannot tell which closed period they hit.

## What the evidence does not tell us

Three gaps limit how much weight the figures can bear.

1. **The survey covers only current members.** These are the people who already manage to reach us at the times we open. The people a new session would help most are those who cannot come now, and they were not asked.
2. **The gap between the two preferences is four people.** With 84 respondents and multiple answers allowed, 35 against 31 is not a clear preference for either option.
3. **The weekday evening answer is ambiguous.** We already open on Thursday evening. A member who ticked "weekday evenings" may want a second evening, or may simply value the one we have. A member who ticked "Sunday" was asking for something we do not offer.

The referral figure has the same weakness. Twelve missed referrals shows there is unmet demand outside our hours, but not which hours.

## Options considered

**1. No change.** This costs nothing and risks nothing. It also leaves the twelve missed referrals and the survey requests unanswered, and it teaches us nothing for the next schedule decision.

**2. Add a Sunday trial (recommended).** It is costed and funded for eight sessions, and the captains' offer covers it exactly.

**3. Add a second weekday evening.** The captains could staff this as easily as a Sunday. However, no cost has been worked out for it, so the board could not approve it this month with a known price. The survey support for it is also the less clear of the two, for the reason given above.

**4. Replace Tuesday noon with a new session.** Tuesday is the quietest session, at about 9 visits. Moving it would free a lease day and coordinator time. But 122 visits last quarter were made by people we know little about. If they are mostly people who can only come in the daytime, closing Tuesday would remove access for them in order to add it for others. We should not make that trade without knowing who the Tuesday visitors are, and the measurement proposed below will tell us.

## Why Sunday, and why eight weeks

Sunday is the only option that is costed, funded, staffed and unambiguous in the survey. That is a practical argument more than proof of demand. Saturday's high attendance may mean weekend demand is strong, or it may mean Saturday already meets it. The trial exists to find out which.

Running the trial weekly for eight consecutive Sundays is better than spreading the same eight sessions over sixteen weeks. People build a visiting habit around a session they can count on every week, and a fortnightly pattern is easier to forget and harder for partners to refer into. The weekly pattern also matches the captains' offer exactly.

The board should be aware of two consequences.

- **Sunday uses the last lease day.** While Sunday runs, a second weekday evening is only possible by closing something else.
- **Success creates a funding question.** The budget covers eight of the roughly twenty-six Sundays in six months. Continuing for the remaining eighteen would cost about 2,520 that is not currently budgeted.

## How we will know whether access improved

Counting Sunday visits is not enough. If twenty people come on Sunday and fifteen of them would otherwise have come on Saturday, the shop is busier on Sunday and access has barely changed. The measures below are designed to separate new access from moved visits.

**1. One question at sign-in, at every session.** Each visitor is asked: "Could you have come at one of our other opening times this week?" The answer is tallied as yes or no, alongside whether this is their first visit. Asking at all four sessions, not only on Sunday, also shows how many Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday visitors have no alternative. That is the information the board lacks for option 4.

**2. Whole-week visit totals.** The baseline is about 42 visits a week across three sessions. We track the weekly total across all four, and watch Saturday in particular for a drop that matches Sunday's gain.

**3. A referral log with times.** Partners are asked to note the day and time of every referral, and we record whether the person was seen. This starts at once and continues for the full six months, whatever happens to Sunday. By the next schedule decision we will know when the missed referrals fall.

**Proposed pass marks.** These are measured over Sundays three to eight, leaving the first two weeks for word to spread.

| Test | Pass mark | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Attendance | Average of 12 or more visits per Sunday | Places Sunday between Tuesday (about 9) and Thursday (about 14) |
| New access | At least half of Sunday visitors could not have come at another time, or are first-time visitors | Means at least 6 visits per session that would not otherwise have happened |
| Displacement | Combined weekly visits at the three existing sessions stay at 38 or above | Allows a drop of about 10% from the baseline of 42 before treating Sunday as mostly moved visits |

The exact numbers are a matter of judgement and the board may wish to adjust them. What matters is that they are fixed before the first Sunday, so the result is read against a standard set in advance.

**Limits of the comparison.** Attendance changes with the season, so last quarter is an imperfect baseline. Six sessions is also a small sample. A result close to any pass mark should be treated as unclear, and the board should then weigh it alongside the referral log and the captains' experience of the sessions.

## What happens after the trial

- **All three tests pass.** The board considers funding Sunday for the remainder of the six months, at about 140 a session, and asks the captains whether they can sustain the commitment.
- **Attendance passes but new access fails.** Sunday is convenient but is not reaching new people. The board should not fund it from access money, and may consider whether a different slot would do better.
- **Attendance fails.** Sunday ends. The remaining lease day stays free, and the referral log and sign-in data guide the next proposal, including a costed second evening.

Sunday sessions will pause between the eighth session and the board's review. The trial should be announced as eight weeks from the start, so that members and partners are not surprised by the pause.

## Risks

- **Volunteer cover has no slack.** If a captain is unavailable, that Sunday has no cover. The rule should be that the session is cancelled with notice, not absorbed by the coordinator. More than one cancellation would weaken the results, and the board should be told if it happens.
- **The 140 figure needs confirming.** This memo assumes it covers the full cost of opening on a Sunday, including any coordinator time that falls outside the captains' shifts. The treasurer should confirm this before the vote. If it does not, the trial as costed will not fit the budget.
- **Sign-in recording adds a small task to every session.** It is one question and a tally mark, but it only works if every session lead does it consistently. A single shared tally sheet, introduced before the first week, should be enough.
- **Raised expectations.** Some members will come to rely on Sunday. Clear communication that this is a trial with a fixed end date reduces the cost of stopping.

## Motions for the board

1. Confirm Tuesday noon, Thursday evening and Saturday morning as fixed sessions for the next six months.
2. Approve a weekly Sunday session for eight consecutive weeks, at a cost not exceeding 1,120 from the trial budget, staffed by the two volunteer captains in alternation.
3. Adopt the sign-in question at all sessions and the timed referral log with partners, both starting in the first week of the new schedule.
4. Adopt the three pass marks set out above, or amended figures agreed at this meeting, as the standard for the review.
5. Schedule the review for the first board meeting after the eighth Sunday, and ask the treasurer to bring a costing for continuing Sunday and for a second weekday evening to that meeting.

# Board decision memo

**Decision requested this month.** Approve a six-month schedule that keeps Tuesday noon, Thursday evening, and Saturday morning, and adds eight Sunday morning sessions on alternate weeks during the first 16 weeks. Authorize up to **1,120 currency units** for the eight sessions. Keep the paid coordinator’s working week at 32 hours. After the eighth Sunday, return to the three regular openings for the balance of the six months unless the board separately approves and funds an extension.

The purpose of the trial is to find out how many people can use the shop because it opens on Sunday, and what happens to people who still cannot get there. The board should agree on the measures and decision rules this month, before it sees the first attendance figures. Members can then plan around a published calendar, and the board can judge the result against the reason it spent the money.

## Why keep the three regular openings

Last quarter the shop recorded 543 visits across the three opening times. Saturday morning accounted for 243, about 45 percent. Thursday evening accounted for 178, about 33 percent, and Tuesday noon accounted for 122, about 22 percent. Saturday has the highest recorded use and Thursday already provides a well-used evening option. Tuesday serves people who can come during a weekday. Removing it would put an established opportunity at risk before the cooperative knows whether those visitors could use another session.

These figures count visits. One person may account for several, and the totals give no count of people who wanted to visit while the doors were closed. The number of sessions actually held in each time slot was also not supplied. For the trial, the shop should record openings and cancellations so that the board can compare visits per session as well as totals. Keeping the existing pattern gives members continuity and makes changes in use easier to interpret.

## Why test Sunday first

Of 84 surveyed members, 35 wanted Sundays and 31 wanted weekday evenings. Members could select both. The four-response difference is too small to settle the choice, and adding the two counts would double-count anyone who selected both options. The survey also leaves a practical question about evenings. Some respondents may be able to use Thursday already, while others may need a different weekday. A second evening deserves consideration if the Sunday trial leaves that need unmet.

Sunday merits the first test because it offers a day the cooperative currently does not open, a substantial group expressed interest, and the board knows the session cost. Sunday morning is a scheduling choice for the pilot. Members were asked about the day, so the board should treat the morning start as an assumption to test. Use the same opening and closing times as Saturday morning to give members a familiar window. Ask people who request Sunday but cannot use the published hours what time they could attend. That will help distinguish a poor choice of hours from weak demand for the day.

The 12 partner referrals that arrived while the shop was closed establish a separate access problem. Their arrival times were not recorded. Any number from zero to 12 might have benefited from a Sunday opening. The cooperative should improve referral records across the whole week, including during the weeks between Sunday sessions. A referral log that covers only trial hours would conceal precisely the gaps the board needs to understand.

## Calendar, staffing, and spending authority

Schedule the first Sunday in the second week of the six-month period, then every other week through week 16. Each trial week uses four opening days, within the lease limit. All other weeks have the three regular openings. Before announcing the pilot, put the eight dates and exact hours on one calendar, alongside the regular schedule and a clear final Sunday date. Give the same calendar to partners, post it at the shop, and use it wherever members ordinarily check opening times. A list of dates is easier to act on than a notice that says “alternate Sundays.”

Assign four dates to each volunteer captain, alternating the lead role. Each captain would then lead one Sunday every four weeks, within the stated capacity of one extra shift per fortnight. That assignment covers leadership. Before publishing a date, the captain must also confirm the volunteers needed to run the shop under its usual staffing practice, including opening and closing. If the practice requires both captains, confirm both for each of the eight dates. That would use their full extra availability. Verify that the regular shifts remain covered in either case.

Eight sessions at 140 currency units each cost 1,120, leaving 80 of the 1,200 trial budget. A ninth would bring the cost to 1,260. The authorization should cover only the eight listed sessions, with actual expenditure recorded against each date. Captains should handle the Sunday tally and closing record as part of their shifts. Assign a board member to compile the figures and obtain the partners’ summaries. Confirm before launch that any coordination required fits within the coordinator’s existing 32 hours. If coverage falls through, notify members and partners promptly and record the cancellation. The coordinator should have no obligation to fill the gap.

## How to tell whether access improves

**Count people who gained a usable opening.** At each Sunday visit, offer one short, optional question: “If the shop had been closed today, could you have come to Tuesday noon, Thursday evening, or Saturday morning for this repair within the next two weeks?” Record yes, no, unsure, or no answer. Two weeks covers a full cycle of the trial. Count a visitor answering “no” as reporting an access gain. A “yes” can still indicate a valued convenience. Keeping that answer visible will let the board see how much of Sunday use came from people who already had a workable option.

Count each person reporting a gain once across the pilot. A simple way is to ask a second question after a “no” answer: “Have we already counted you on an earlier Sunday as someone who couldn’t come at another time?” Record repeat and uncertain responses separately. This produces an estimate based on visitors’ own answers without requiring names. Report the counts of unanswered and uncertain responses alongside the estimate. Also record whether the visitor received repair assistance or had to leave without being helped. A person who found an opening but could not get help reveals a different problem from a person who could not get through the door.

**Track use across the whole schedule.** For every opening, record the date, time slot, visits, and any cancellation or unusual disruption. At review, show weekly visits across all days, visits per held session for each time slot, and separate results for weeks with and without a Sunday. Compare the regular sessions with last quarter where the records support a like-for-like comparison. A drop on Saturday alongside a busy Sunday may suggest that people moved their visits. Some of those people may still have gained access, particularly if they could not attend Saturday that fortnight. Read the attendance pattern together with the visitor answers. Seasonal changes and differences between weeks limit what the totals alone can establish.

**Follow referrals through to an outcome.** Ask partners to record the day and time a person tried to use the shop, if known, and whether the shop was open. Record the time the partner sent the referral separately if it differs. Using an agreed reference without a name in the board report, record whether the person received assistance within two weeks, was still waiting, or had an unknown outcome. Include the total number of referrals so the board can interpret the number arriving during closures. Continue the log throughout all six months. The closing weeks will show which gaps persist once the Sunday trial ends. The earlier 12 cases supply context, but their missing times and the unknown total referral volume prevent a reliable before-and-after rate.

## Review and decision rules

After the fourth scheduled Sunday, the designated board member should check the records with the captains and partners. Confirm that members can find the dates, shifts have been covered, spending is on track, and the access question is being asked consistently. Correct problems while there are still four sessions left. If an opening is cancelled or the tally is incomplete, retain that fact in the report. Four poorly advertised sessions would tell the board as much about how it announced the trial as about members’ ability to attend.

For this pilot, adopt **16 distinct visitors who report gaining access and receive repair assistance** as the threshold for considering a Sunday extension. That is an average of two people newly able to get help per planned session. At the full authorized spend, meeting the threshold would cost 70 currency units per such person. This is a proposed board judgment about what the trial should achieve, rather than an estimate derived from the survey. Report the actual spend and actual count together. If nobody meets the definition, report zero people helped on this measure and omit the cost-per-person calculation.

At the first board meeting after the eighth scheduled Sunday, consider an extension if the trial meets the threshold, regular openings remained staffed, and the coordinator’s hours held at 32. Review outstanding referrals and people turned away alongside the headline count. Before authorizing more dates, identify the funding and confirm a sustainable roster. If the trial falls short despite reliable delivery and good response coverage, keep the three regular openings and use the recorded days and times to assess a different weekday evening or a different Sunday window. If cancellations or missing responses leave the result inconclusive, record that uncertainty. The calendar still reverts to three days, and another trial would require its own proposal.

At six months, the board should receive a one-page closeout showing sessions planned and held, actual spending, the number of distinct visitors who gained access and received assistance, and the timing and outcomes of partner referrals. Include the times most often requested by people who still could not attend. This gives the board a basis for its next schedule decision and gives members a concrete account of what the eight extra openings achieved.

feb9c33905269e4f.text:
# Board decision memo — Opening schedule for the next six months

## Decision requested this month

Keep the Tuesday noon, Thursday evening, and Saturday morning openings for the full six months. Authorize eight Sunday morning trial sessions, held every other week from 10 a.m. to noon, beginning on the first Sunday of the new schedule. Review the trial in month five, before committing to any further Sunday openings. Publish all eight dates together so members and referral partners can plan around them.

Authorize up to 1,120 currency units for the trial, based on eight sessions at 140 each. This leaves 80 of the 1,200 trial budget uncommitted. Ask the two volunteer captains to alternate Sundays, with each covering four sessions, and confirm that the full roster and the coordinator’s duties fit within existing commitments before publishing the dates. Keep the paid coordinator’s working week at 32 hours.

The recurring schedule returns to the three existing openings after the eighth Sunday unless the board approves and funds an extension. Set the review date when adopting the schedule so the board has time to act before the six-month period ends.

## Why this schedule

The three current openings drew 543 visits last quarter. Saturday morning accounted for 243, Thursday evening for 178, and Tuesday noon for 122. These are visit totals, and repeat visitors may account for some of them. The figures also lack the number and duration of sessions held, which limits comparisons of attendance per opening. They do establish that people use all three slots. Keeping them preserves the access people already rely on while the cooperative tests an additional day.

Among 84 surveyed members, 35 selected Sundays and 31 selected weekday evenings. Members could select more than one answer, so some of the same people may have chosen both. The four-response difference is too small to carry the decision on its own, and the survey does not establish how often respondents would attend. Sunday gives the cooperative a chance to test a day it currently misses. A second weekday evening would test whether another evening is useful alongside Thursday. That remains a credible option, particularly if trial visitors and referral partners report weekday evening demand that Thursday cannot meet.

The twelve partner referrals that arrived while the shop was closed show a gap worth tracking. Their arrival times were never recorded, so the board cannot tell which schedule change, if any, would have helped those people. Use the trial to learn when new referrals arrive, when referred people are able to attend, and whether Sunday helps them complete a visit. With only twelve known cases last quarter, report referral results as counts with context and use them alongside visitor feedback.

The proposed 10 a.m. to noon window gives the trial a consistent, easy-to-publish time. The survey asked about Sunday as a day and does not establish a preferred time. Treat the result as evidence about alternate Sunday mornings. A weak result would leave open whether weekly Sundays, a different Sunday time, or another weekday evening would serve more people.

## Cost and staffing

Eight sessions cost 1,120. A ninth would bring the total to 1,260, above the trial budget. Eight sessions spread over roughly four months give members repeated chances to attend and leave the board time to review the evidence within the six-month schedule. In weeks with a Sunday session, the shop opens on four days, within the lease limit. In other weeks, it opens on three.

Alternating Sundays gives each captain one extra shift every four weeks under the proposed roster, within their stated capacity of one extra shift per fortnight. Before announcing dates, confirm the captains’ availability, any other volunteers required to run a normal session, and who will handle opening, closing, and recording visits. Identify the coordinator’s scheduling, communications, and reporting tasks and fit them into the existing 32-hour week. Confirm that the 140-per-session estimate covers the planned opening. If the roster, hours, or cost cannot be made to work, bring a reduced trial back to the board before advertising it.

Publish the dates through the channels members already use and give partners the same calendar. Explain that Sunday opens on specific dates, since a person who turns up on the intervening Sunday faces the same access problem the trial is meant to address. If a session loses coverage, notify members and partners promptly. Record cancellations, actual costs, and staffing problems so the board can distinguish limited demand from limited delivery.

## How to measure access

The primary measure is the number of distinct people who receive repair help on a trial Sunday and say they could not have used Tuesday noon, Thursday evening, or Saturday morning during the same fortnight. Count each person once toward this measure across the trial. A Sunday visit can be valuable even when a person could have attended another day, but the board needs to know how often the extra opening makes a visit possible. The fortnight is the comparison period because that is how often the new slot is offered.

Keep the check-in short. At a Sunday visit, ask whether the person could have used any of the three regular openings that fortnight, with options for yes, no, and unsure. Record whether they received repair help, whether they came through a partner referral, and whether this is their first Sunday visit during the trial. Use the existing check-in system to identify repeat visitors where possible. Keep missing and unsure answers visible in the report. The access measure depends on what people report about their availability, so present it as an estimate of who gained access.

Track total visits and the number of sessions actually held for each opening, including the three regular slots. Bring visits per session to the review and show results both with and without the first Sunday, so the board can see whether initial turnout persisted. Where comparable historical session counts are available, include them. Look for changes in regular attendance, staffing or service interruptions, and people who had to leave without help. A move from Saturday to Sunday can relieve crowding, if the shop observes it. Report that effect separately from access for people who could not attend before.

Give referral partners a simple way to note the date and time of each referral attempt and, if they know it, which openings the person can use. At the shop, record whether the person arrived and received help. Summarize how many referrals were made during closed hours, how many resulted in a visit, and how many reached the shop on Sunday. A referral can arrive during closed hours and still lead to a Thursday or Saturday visit, so the outcome matters as much as the timestamp. Ask partners to mention timing barriers they hear from people who never reach the shop. That feedback can reveal gaps a visitor survey will miss.

## What would justify continuing

Adopt a review rule before the first session. Recommend continuing alternate Sunday mornings only if the trial meets all three conditions:

- **At least 24 distinct people gained access** under the primary measure. Across eight sessions, that is three people per scheduled session on average. At the planned cost of 1,120, it amounts to about 47 currency units per person who gained access. This is a proposed threshold for the board to adopt as a spending judgment.
- **At least eight of those people first gained access during the final four sessions.** This gives the board evidence of demand beyond the launch and still allows for a stronger response when the schedule is first announced.
- **The cooperative can sustain the opening.** An extension needs a confirmed volunteer roster and funding, a workable plan within the coordinator’s 32-hour week, and the ability to deliver all three regular openings reliably.

At the month-five meeting, put actual spending, sessions delivered, and the number of people who gained access on the same page. Include the cost per person who gained access, the number of missing or uncertain availability responses, and a brief account of how regular openings and referral outcomes changed. Show the counts behind each conclusion. Eight sessions can support a practical scheduling decision, with limited confidence about seasonal changes or demand at other times.

If the trial meets the conditions, vote on a funded extension with dates and a named staffing plan. If it falls short, let the authorization expire and retain the three regular slots for the balance of the six months. If cancellations or missing responses made the result hard to interpret, explain that at the review and require a fresh decision and budget for any further test. Use recorded timing barriers to decide whether a later trial should test a different Sunday time or a second weekday evening.

## Proposed motion

The board adopts Tuesday noon, Thursday evening, and Saturday morning as the cooperative’s regular opening schedule for the next six months. It authorizes eight alternate Sunday trials from 10 a.m. to noon, beginning on the first Sunday of the schedule, at a total cost of up to 1,120 currency units. The Sunday dates will be published after staffing and cost are confirmed within existing volunteer capacity and the coordinator’s 32-hour workweek. The board adopts the access measures and continuation criteria in this memo and will review the results in month five. Sunday opening authority expires after the eighth trial session. Any extension requires a separate board vote and confirmed funding.
